'''Brian Glüss''' [[Royal Statistical Society|FRSS]] (23 August 1930 – 26 December 2013) was a statistician, mathematician, systems engineer and author.<ref name="auto">''Who's Who in America'', 2010, 64th Edition (pub.2009)</ref><ref>''Who's Who in American Education'', 2007–2008, 8th edition (pub. 2007)</ref><ref>''Who's Who in Science and Engineering'', 2008–2009, 10th edition (pub.2007)</ref><ref name="auto1">Obituary, ''Brian Gluss'', [[Pembroke College, Cambridge|Pembroke College]], Cambridge Society, Annual Gazette, Issue 89, September 2015</ref><ref name="auto2">Obituary, ''Dr Brian Glüss'', ''Eagle News'', The Magazine of the [[Bedford Modern School|Old Bedford Modernians’ Club]], New Series, Volume 6, Number 3 (Issue 110), January 2015</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.worldcat.org/search?q=au:Gluss,%20Brian.&qt=hot_author|title=Results for 'au:Gluss, Brian.' [WorldCat.org]|accessdate=30 April 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9BHvAAAAMAAJ&q=brian%20gluss|title=World Directory of Mathematicians|date=1 January 1990|publisher=School of Mathematics, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research|accessdate=30 April 2017|via=Google Books}}</ref> He also became an expert on victims of violent death in war and peace, on the process of healing their families and on the condition of [[survivor guilt]].<ref name="auto1"/><ref name="auto2"/>

==Early life==
Brian Glüss was born in London on 23 August 1930, the son of Joseph Glüss and Otilie (née Tenenhaus).<ref name="auto"/><ref name="auto1"/> His father, known as "Mottle", was from Russia and his mother, known as "Tilly", was from Botosani in Romania. They were all Jewish. In 1940, the family suffered tragedy when their London home was hit by a German bomb killing Glüss's grandmother Anna Tenenhaus nee Goldshlager and his brother, Michael.<ref name="auto1"/> The family moved to [[Bedford]] and Glüss was educated in the town at [[Bedford Modern School]] where he excelled.<ref name="auto1"/><ref name="auto2"/> After National Service with the Royal Air Force, Glüss went up to [[Pembroke College, Cambridge]], on a state scholarship, matriculating in 1949 and taking the Mathematical Tripos.<ref name="auto"/><ref name="auto1"/> On graduation he was made a Pembroke Foundation Scholar and he took the Diploma in Mathematical Statistics in 1953.<ref name="auto1"/>

==Career==
On leaving [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]], Glüss was made research assistant to [[Maurice Kendall|Professor Maurice Kendall]] (later Sir Maurice Kendall), an esteemed statistician who was then at the [[London School of Economics]].<ref name="auto1"/> After the LSE he worked as an actuarial clerk at Prudential Assurance in London before leaving England for America in 1954 having been contracted to work on the Jury Project at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="auto1"/> At the end of his contract he went to [[Ottawa]] as an Assistant to the Senior Researcher in the Bureau of Statistics of the Canadian Government between 1956 and 1958.<ref name="auto"/> At the end of his tenure at Ottawa, he returned to Chicago and became a staff member at the [[Illinois Institute of Technology]] between 1958 and 1962 before studying for a PhD in Electrical Engineering at [[University of California, Berkeley|Berkeley University]]; he was awarded his PhD in 1965.<ref name="auto"/>

After Berkeley, Glüss moved to [[Santa Monica, California]], where he worked for the [[RAND Corporation]] under [[Richard E. Bellman|Richard Bellman]], an American applied mathematician and pioneer of [[dynamic programming]], a subject on which Glüss wrote 'a well received book'.<ref name="auto"/><ref name="auto1"/> Following his time at the [[RAND Corporation]] he was made a Professor at the [[University of Illinois at Chicago]] and, later, Emeritus Professor following his retirement in 1988.<ref name="auto"/>

==Work on survivor guilt and charitable causes==
Glüss didn't speak about the tragic circumstances that had befallen his family until he was 25, but instead found consolation in the work of [[William Guglielmo Niederland|William Niederland]], a New York psychoanalyst who had observed, examined and worked with 2,000 survivors of the [[Nazi concentration camps]].<ref name="auto"/><ref name="auto2"/> Writing to his old school in 2006 about his own experience and his respect for [[William Guglielmo Niederland|Niederland]], Glüss commented:

<blockquote>To varying degrees, he [Niederland] found a bundle of common symptoms, which he later termed survivor guilt.  Then, in the 1950s, he went on to examine peacetime survivors, in the US, who had lost loved ones to violent death in peacetime, by murder, suicide, violent accident.  Again, in varying degrees, the same symptoms cropped up.  Discovering Neiderland was the key to my final recovery.  Without him I’d still be in generalized grief.  When I work with survivors, I use his method</blockquote>

Inspired by [[William Guglielmo Niederland|Niederland]], Glüss used his own experiences to help others in one-on-one work with other survivors.<ref name="auto2"/> He engaged in voluntary work in retirement homes in Berkeley, California, and was a voluntary mentor for victims of grief.<ref name="auto"/>

==Personal life==
Whilst at [[University of California, Berkeley|Berkeley]], Glüss married Joan Marie Chodorow, a therapist.<ref name="auto"/><ref name="auto1"/> The marriage was difficult and ended in divorce but he was fond of his stepchild, Lori Kim Smallwood.<ref name="auto1"/> A life already beset by tragedy, his stepdaughter was murdered in 1980 which led to Glüss campaigning against handgun ownership; his writings influenced the San Francisco and Berkeley gun control ordinances of 1982.<ref name="auto1"/> After that sad event and retirement, he devoted his life to charitable and political causes; the tragedies he'd faced ‘did not diminish his cheerfulness and optimism’.<ref name="auto1"/> He died on [[Boxing Day]] 2013 in Berkeley.<ref name="auto1"/>

==Selected works==
* ''An elementary introduction to dynamic programming; a state equation approach''. Published by [[Allyn & Bacon]], [[Boston]], USA, 1972<ref>{{cite book|title=An elementary introduction to dynamic programming; a state equation approach.|first=Brian|last=Gluss|date=1 January 1972|publisher=Allyn and Bacon|oclc = 278091}}</ref>
* ''Invariant imbedding and the solution of differential equations''.  Published by the [[RAND Corporation]], [[Santa Monica, California]], USA, 1966<ref>{{cite book|title=Invariant imbedding and the solution of differential equations|first=Brian|last=Gluss|date=1 January 1966|publisher=Rand Corp.|oclc = 22404707}}</ref>
* ''A diffusion-equation model for neuron firing with exponential decay of potential''.  Published by the [[RAND Corporation]], [[Santa Monica, California]], 1966<ref>{{cite book|title=A diffusion-equation model for neuron firing with exponential decay of potential|first=Brian|last=Gluss|date=1 January 1966|publisher=Rand Corp.|oclc = 22416645}}</ref>
* ''Generalizations of the two-armed bandit problem''.  Dissertation for the [[University of California, Berkeley]], 1965<ref>{{cite book|title=Generalizations of the two-armed bandit problem.|first=Brian|last=Gluss|date=1 January 1965|oclc = 20215876}}</ref>
